nameStory: The Fourspine Stickleback gets its name from the four sharp spines along its back that can prick your fingers if you handle it carelessly. It's also called the 'bloody stickleback' - not because it's aggressive, but because males develop brilliant red coloring on their bellies during breeding season that looks like they've been painted with bright red paint.
description: This small, slender fish is one of New England's most distinctive little swimmers, rarely growing longer than your index finger. Its body has a narrow, almost torpedo-like shape with four prominent spines sticking up from its back like tiny sail masts. During breeding season, males transform from dull brownish-green to show off stunning red undersides, while females stay more subdued in their olive-brown coloring.

idTips.label: Spines
idTips.description: Four sharp, separate spines along the back that you can feel poking through the water when netting - they're stiff and won't fold down like a regular fin

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Slim, elongated body that feels firm and muscular when gently held, with a distinctly narrow tail section that tapers dramatically

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Tiny fish, typically 2-3 inches long - about the size of a large minnow but with that unmistakable spiny back

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Males in breeding season show bright red bellies that look almost artificial, while non-breeding fish appear olive-brown with darker mottling

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Small, translucent fins that feel delicate to touch, with the tail fin having a slightly squared-off shape rather than deeply forked

habitat: Look for Fourspine Sticklebacks in shallow, weedy areas of coastal ponds, salt marshes, and the brackish zones where rivers meet the sea. They love areas with plenty of aquatic vegetation where they can dart in and out of cover, particularly in water that's calm and relatively warm.

seasonality.spring: Males begin developing their brilliant red breeding colors and become very territorial, building small nest areas in shallow vegetation. This is the best time to spot their dramatic coloration.
seasonality.summer: Peak breeding season when males are at their most colorful and active. You'll often see them chasing each other through the shallows in elaborate courtship displays.
seasonality.fall: Breeding colors fade and fish school together more peacefully. They begin moving to slightly deeper water as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Much less active and harder to spot, often hiding deep in vegetation or moving to the deepest parts of their habitat to wait out the cold.

funFact: Male Fourspine Sticklebacks are such dedicated fathers that they actually fan their eggs with their fins to keep fresh, oxygenated water flowing over them, and will attack fish many times their size - even your finger - to defend their nest!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the Threespine Stickleback, but counting the spines is your foolproof method - four spines means Fourspine, three means Threespine. Memory trick: 'Four for the shore' since Fourspines prefer shallower coastal waters.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'stickleback' comes from the Old English meaning 'prickly back,' and these fish have been used in classic animal behavior studies because of their elaborate courtship rituals and nest-building behaviors.
compareHints: Since the Fourspine Stickleback is the only species in its genus, compare it to other sticklebacks in the family - it has more spines than the common Threespine Stickleback and prefers more brackish, coastal waters. Unlike the Ninespine Stickleback which has many tiny spines, the Fourspine has exactly four prominent, well-separated spines that are easy to count.
